title: Hot partitions, rebalancing and resharding without downtime
scopeHtml: Scope: hot keys, rebalancing strategies, online resharding, capacity planning. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: What a hot partition is
notes.html:
A hot partition is one shard that receives far more traffic than the others, so it becomes the bottleneck while the rest sit idle. Adding more shards does not help because the extra capacity is not where the load is.

Causes:

  • Hot key: one celebrity user, one viral product, one flash-sale item.
  • Skewed key distribution: sequential keys on range partitions, one giant tenant.
  • Time-based hotspot: everyone reads "today's" partition.
  • Bad hashing luck: a few shards randomly get more big keys.

How it looks in production: one node at 95% CPU while the cluster averages 20%; p99 latency spikes on a subset of requests; throttling errors on one partition (DynamoDB ProvisionedThroughputExceededException even though table-level capacity looks fine); one Redis node with a huge instantaneous_ops_per_sec.

Worked example. A cluster of 10 shards each handling up to 10k ops/s (100k total). A viral post gets 40k reads/s, all on its single shard: that shard saturates at 10k and drops 75% of requests, while the cluster as a whole uses only 40% of its capacity.

Industry examples. Twitter faced celebrity accounts (very high fan-out); Instagram handles celebrity feeds differently from normal users; DynamoDB documents "hot partitions" and added adaptive capacity to shift throughput to hot partitions (confirm limits in current docs, one partition is still capped at about 3,000 read and 1,000 write units per second).

Everyday analogy. A supermarket with 10 checkout lanes where everyone queues at lane 3 because the only cashier who sells lottery tickets sits there.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling it a capacity problem and answering "add shards".
  • Not distinguishing a hot key (cannot be split by hashing) from a hot range (can be split).
  • Not naming the metric: per-partition ops, not cluster average.

notes.title: Detecting and fixing hot keys
notes.html:
Detection: per-key counters sampled (Redis redis-cli --hotkeys needs an LFU policy; MONITOR is too expensive in prod), per-partition metrics, proxy-level sampling (Twemproxy, Envoy), top-N sketches (count-min sketch) in the app.

Fixes, cheapest first:

  1. Cache in front. A local in-process cache with a 1 to 5 s TTL on the hot key removes most reads.
  2. Replicate the hot key. Store copies under key#0 .. key#9; readers pick a random one. Reads spread over 10 shards.
  3. Salting writes. For a counter, write to likes:post42:{0..9} randomly and sum on read (or aggregate in the background). Writes spread; reads cost 10 lookups or a periodic rollup.
  4. Request coalescing (single-flight). On cache miss only one request goes to the database; others wait for it. Prevents stampedes.
  5. Isolate: put the known whale on its own shard (directory-based mapping).
  6. Queue and batch writes. Buffer increments and flush every second.
import random
N = 10  # copies of the hot key
def read_hot(key):
    return redis.get(f"{key}#{random.randrange(N)}")
def write_hot(key, val):
    for i in range(N):
        redis.set(f"{key}#{i}", val)

Worked example. A flash-sale product row gets 30k reads/s on one MySQL shard. Add a 2 s local cache across 50 app servers: each server hits the DB at most 0.5 times/s for that key, so about 25 reads/s total (a 1,200x reduction). Stale for at most 2 s, acceptable for a product page, not for stock count at checkout.

Decision gravity. Key replication and salting are reversible app-level changes, but add read or write amplification and consistency complexity. Cache is the cheapest. Isolating a tenant via directory is also reversible.

Industry examples. Memcached/Facebook "leases" prevent thundering herd; Redis Cluster users often append hash tags or random suffixes; Discord coalesces identical requests to Cassandra in its data services so a hot channel produces one query.

Everyday analogy. Printing 10 copies of the popular notice and pinning them in different corridors instead of one on the main door.

Common interview traps.

  • Salting counters and forgetting the read cost.
  • Caching hot items without TTL or invalidation thinking, then serving stale prices.
  • Not mentioning the cache stampede when a hot key expires.

notes.title: Rebalancing: moving data between shards
notes.html:
Rebalancing moves partitions from busy or full nodes to others, after nodes are added, removed or the load shifts. The constraints: keep serving traffic, limit network use, and not lose or duplicate writes.

Strategies:

  • Fixed number of partitions (many more partitions than nodes): create, say, 1,024 partitions up front; a new node steals some partitions whole. Used by Elasticsearch (primary shard count fixed at index creation), Kafka (partitions), Riak, Couchbase (vBuckets), Redis Cluster (slots).
  • Dynamic splitting: a partition splits when it grows past a size (for example 10 GB) or load. HBase, Bigtable, MongoDB chunks (balancer migrates chunks), CockroachDB ranges (512 MiB default range size, confirm in docs).
  • Proportional to nodes: Cassandra vnodes: each new node takes random token ranges.

Automatic vs manual: automatic rebalancing is convenient but can surprise you, because moving data during a load spike makes the spike worse and a falsely detected node failure can trigger a storm of copying. Many teams require a human to approve or throttle.

Worked example. 3 nodes with 48 partitions total (16 each), 300 GB each. Add node D: target is 12 each, so each old node gives 4 partitions (about 75 GB), 225 GB moves in total. On a 1 Gbps (about 100 MB/s usable) link capped at 50% for the migration: 225,000 MB / 50 MB/s = 4,500 s, about 75 minutes. Throttle with stream_throughput_outbound (Cassandra) or MongoDB balancer windows.

# MongoDB: only balance at night
mongosh --eval 'db.getSiblingDB("config").settings.updateOne(
  {_id:"balancer"},
  {$set:{activeWindow:{start:"01:00",stop:"05:00"}}}, {upsert:true})'

Decision gravity. Over-provisioning partitions up front (fixed count) is cheap insurance and reversible. Too many partitions add overhead (each Kafka partition and Elasticsearch shard costs memory and file handles); too few caps parallelism forever. Elasticsearch fixed primary shard count is effectively a one-way door (needs reindex or split API).

Industry examples. Kafka partition reassignment (kafka-reassign-partitions.sh, Cruise Control automates it), Elasticsearch shard allocation, MongoDB balancer, Cassandra nodetool rebuild/bootstrap, CockroachDB automatic range rebalancing.

Everyday analogy. Moving students from crowded classrooms to a new classroom by whole benches, not by tearing benches apart.

Common interview traps.

  • Using hash % N and then proposing to "just add a node".
  • Ignoring that rebalancing competes with live traffic for disk and network.
  • Setting 10,000 tiny partitions "to be safe", producing overhead.

notes.title: Resharding without downtime
notes.html:
Resharding means changing how data is split (more shards, or a different key) while the system stays up. The standard pattern is dual write plus backfill plus cutover:

  1. Provision new shards (target layout).
  2. Backfill: copy existing data from old shards to new in the background, throttled. Take a consistent snapshot or record the position (binlog/WAL offset).
  3. Catch up: stream changes since the snapshot (CDC with Debezium, Vitess VReplication, MongoDB change streams) so new shards track old ones.
  4. Verify: compare row counts and checksums; optionally shadow-read from the new shards and diff results.
  5. Cutover: briefly stop writes (seconds) or use a routing flag per shard, flip reads then writes to the new layout.
  6. Keep old as fallback (reverse replication) for days, then delete.

Variations:

  • Split in place (doubling): each old shard splits into two, children get half the hash range. Easy with power-of-two logical shards because every key's new home is deterministic. Instagram-style logical shards are designed so physical moves only copy a logical shard.
  • Double-write at app level: the app writes to both old and new for the new key space. Simple but you must handle partial failures (write to old succeeds, new fails) via outbox/retry.
  • Feature flag per tenant/key range to migrate gradually and roll back one at a time.

Worked example. Move from 4 to 8 shards, 2 TB total. Backfill 500 GB per old shard at 40 MB/s = about 3.5 hours each; CDC lag shrinks to under 1 s; cutover with a 3-second write pause per shard behind a router flag (flip shard_map.state from MIGRATING to ACTIVE). Total user-visible disruption: a few seconds of elevated latency per shard.

# Vitess-style MoveTables workflow (illustrative stages)
steps:
  - create: copy schema to target keyspace
  - vreplication: copy plus stream binlog
  - verify: VDiff compare
  - switch_reads
  - switch_writes
  - complete: drop source

Industry examples. Vitess MoveTables/Reshard, Stripe's online migration approach (dual writes, shadow reads, then cutover), Shopify's pod mobility moves shops between database pods with minimal downtime using Ghostferry, Notion's 2021 resharding from 32 to 480 logical shards using Postgres logical replication, GitHub gh-ost for online schema change.

Decision gravity. Dual write and CDC are reversible until the cutover step; cutover is the commit point, so keep reverse replication ready. Changing the shard key (rather than the count) is the hardest, because all queries and indexes change; it is a one-way door in practice.

Everyday analogy. Moving house while living there: carry boxes over a few weeks, keep both addresses working, then switch the mail forwarding on one day.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting writes that happen during backfill (need CDC or dual write).
  • No verification step before cutover.
  • No rollback plan.
  • Dual writes without handling partial failure (use outbox or CDC instead).

notes.title: Capacity planning to avoid emergencies
notes.html:
Reshard before you must. Resharding under load, with a full disk, is how outages happen.

Rules of thumb:

  • Alert at 60% of disk, CPU or write IOPS per shard, act at 70%. Resharding takes days to weeks to plan; the data copy needs headroom itself.
  • Pick the logical shard count generously (1,024 or 4,096) so you scale from 4 to 64 machines without changing mapping.
  • Watch growth: with 15% month-on-month data growth, 60% full turns into 100% full in about 4 months.
  • Test the runbook: rehearse resharding on a copy in staging at production scale.
  • Keep a per-shard dashboard: size, QPS, p99, replication lag, top keys.

Worked example. Shard at 1.8 TB of 3 TB disk, growing 100 GB/week: 12 weeks to full. Backfill takes 2 weeks and planning 2 weeks, so start now, not when the alert pages at 90%.

Industry examples. Notion reportedly resharded when Postgres hit vacuum and disk limits; Figma and Slack describe vertical sharding and logical shards as ways to buy time; Pinterest's early sharding used pre-created virtual shards (made when launched) mapped to few servers.

Everyday analogy. Booking a bigger flat before the baby arrives, not the week after.

Common interview traps.

  • Waiting for the disk to fill.
  • Treating resharding as one script instead of a multi-week project with verification and rollback.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Hot partitions come from hot keys, skewed ranges, or time hotspots; more shards do not fix a single hot key.
  • Fix order: cache, replicate hot keys, salt writes, coalesce requests, isolate whales, batch writes.
  • Rebalance with many fixed partitions or dynamic splitting; throttle it and compute the data volume and time.
  • Reshard online: snapshot plus backfill, CDC catch-up, verify, cutover, keep reverse path, then delete.
  • Plan capacity early: alert at 60%, over-provision logical shards, rehearse the runbook.
